subject: gamblers-fallacy
title: Why "Due" Is a Myth
summary: Streaks feel like they must even out. They don't. Where that instinct fails, and where it's right.

keys.prompt: Why isn't tails "due" after a streak of heads from a fair coin?
keys.answer: Flips are independent, so the next flip is still 50/50. A streak is rare in advance, but the past flips are already known.

keys.prompt: Why do people believe streaks must balance out?
keys.answer: They expect short runs to look like the long-run average (the law of small numbers), so they think a streak has to be corrected.
When events are not independent, like drawing cards without putting them back, or when a streak suggests the coin or game is biased.

cards.title: 26 blacks in a row
cards.text: On August 18, 1913, a roulette ball at the Monte Carlo Casino landed on black 26 times in a row. As the streak grew, gamblers kept betting on red, sure the wheel had to "balance out." They lost millions of francs. What was their math missing?

cards.question: You flip a fair coin and get heads 20 times in a row. What is the chance, in percent, that flip number 21 is heads?
cards.reveal: 50%. Twenty heads then another head is exactly as likely as twenty heads then a tail: each is 0.5 to the 21st power, about 1 in 2,097,152.

cards.title: Before vs. after the flips
cards.text: Before you start, five heads in a row has a probability of 1/32, about 3%. But after four heads, those four flips are no longer a mystery. Only the fifth is. "5 heads" and "4 heads, then a tail" are each 1/32, so the next flip is 1/2 either way.

why.q: Why is a streak rare in advance but not "rare" for the next flip?
why.a: The rare part was getting the first flips. Once they are done, the next flip is still a fresh 1/2.

cards.title: The wheel's real odds
cards.text: For a single-zero wheel with 18 black pockets out of 37, a run of 26 of one color (red or black) has a chance of 2 × (18/37)^26. That is about 1 in 68.4 million. Rare, yes. But the gamblers bet as if the wheel had a memory that would force red to come back.

cards.title: The law of small numbers
cards.text: Tversky and Kahneman argued that people use a shortcut called representativeness: they expect even a short run of random results to look like the long-run average. So after many reds, black seems like the more "representative" next result. People asked to invent random coin tosses also keep the heads-to-tails ratio too close to 0.5.

why.q: Why does a short sequence not need to look 50/50?
why.a: Small samples vary a lot. The expectation that every short run balances out is the mistake.

cards.title: Do the "due" math
cards.text: Say you win a game if you roll a 1 on a 16-sided die, and you get 16 rolls. Your chance of at least one win is 1 − (15/16)^16 = 64.39%. After one miss, with 15 rolls left, it is 1 − (15/16)^15 = 62.02%. Losing didn't make a win more likely. It left you fewer chances.

cards.title: When "due" is real
cards.text: Some things do have memory. Draw an ace from a deck and keep it out: the chance the next card is an ace falls from 4/52 (7.69%) to 3/51 (5.88%). That is how card counting works. And some games add a "pity timer" that improves loot box odds after many bad opens. In those, "due" is built in, but it can feed the belief that all random things are due.

cards.question: A friend says, "I've lost 8 bets in a row, so my next one is more likely to win." Argue the case for why they might be wrong, then the case for when they might be right.
nudges: What would you need to know about how the bets work?
Could the streak itself be a clue?
Does it matter if each bet is independent?

questions.q: After 4 heads in a row on a fair coin, what is the probability of heads on flip 5?

options.why: Right. Independence means the next flip is still 1/2.
1/32 was the chance of five heads before any flips. After four are done, the next is 1/2.

options.text: Less than 1/2, since tails is due
options.why: The coin has no memory, so tails isn't due.

options.text: More than 1/2, since heads is hot
options.why: A fair coin doesn't get hot either.

questions.q: Which situation is NOT an example of the gambler's fallacy?

options.text: Expecting a king to be less likely after kings are drawn and kept out of the deck
options.why: Right. Cards drawn without replacement change the odds.

options.text: Expecting black after a long run of red on a fair wheel
options.why: That is the fallacy: the wheel has no memory.

options.text: Expecting tails after four heads on a fair coin
options.why: That is the fallacy: independent flips.

options.text: Raising your bet on red after 10 blacks
options.why: That is the fallacy: independent spins.

questions.q: What is the main idea behind the law of small numbers?

options.text: People expect short runs to look like the long-run average
options.why: Right. That expectation leads to the false idea that streaks must be corrected.

options.text: Small groups always have the same results
options.why: Small samples actually vary a lot.

options.text: Large samples vary more than small ones
options.why: It is the reverse: small samples vary more.
